key_instruments: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689); amended by the 'Digital Omnibus on AI' (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)
scope: all AI systems, with a risk-based tiering (banned practices, high-risk, limited-risk transparency duties, general-purpose AI models); binding across all 27 EU member states
enforcement_mechanism: yes — national market-surveillance authorities plus a new EU AI Office; fines up to 7% of global annual revenue (or €35m) for banned-practice violations, up to 3% for other breaches
effective_date_or_status: Entered into force 1 Aug 2024; banned practices + AI literacy rules applied from 2 Feb 2025; general-purpose AI model rules from 2 Aug 2025; Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) formally adopted by the Council 29 Jun 2026, published in the Official Journal 24 Jul 2026, entered into force 27 Jul 2026 — it pushes standalone high-risk (Annex III) system rules from 2 Aug 2026 to 2 Dec 2027, and high-risk systems embedded in regulated products (Annex I) from 2 Aug 2027 to 2 Aug 2028; Article 50 transparency/labeling duties (e.g. disclosing AI-generated content) are NOT delayed and remain effective 2 Aug 2026 (only the watermarking technical requirement for already-deployed systems gets a 4-month reprieve to 2 Dec 2026)
plain_language_summary: The EU is the first place in the world with a real, binding AI law. It bans a few dangerous uses of AI outright, and for 'high-risk' uses like hiring or credit-scoring tools, companies must test and register the systems before selling them. Fines for breaking the rules can reach 7% of a company's worldwide revenue. In mid-2026 the EU formally passed a 'Digital Omnibus' law that pushed the toughest high-risk-system deadlines back to December 2027 and August 2028 (from August 2026/2027) — but the requirement to label AI-generated content still starts in August 2026 as originally planned.

Agent 1 flagged the post-Omnibus high-risk dates as unconfirmed against a primary source; I confirmed them: the Digital Omnibus on AI was adopted as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, published in the Official Journal 24 Jul 2026, in force 27 Jul 2026 (multiple independent law-firm trackers agree on this citation and on the Dec 2027/Aug 2028 dates, which happen to match the dates Agent 1 had already written). Added the important nuance Agent 1 lacked: Article 50 transparency/AI-content-labeling duties were NOT delayed and still start 2 Aug 2026 — only the harder Annex III/I high-risk obligations were pushed back. Upgraded confidence from medium to high given this is now confirmed against a specific, dated regulation.

key_instruments: Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS 225)
scope: AI systems used by public authorities and private actors, focused on human rights/democracy/rule-of-law impacts; open to non-European countries too
enforcement_mechanism: intended yes once in force (first-ever legally binding international AI treaty) — but not yet in force; each ratifying country sets its own enforcement/oversight body domestically
effective_date_or_status: Opened for signature 5 Sept 2024; needs 5 ratifications (incl. 3 Council of Europe member states) to enter into force; as of 8 Sept 2026 only the EU has ratified (deposited 15 May 2026) and 21 states/organisations have signed — the Convention still has zero Parties and is not in force; Switzerland signed 27 Mar 2025 but has not yet ratified
plain_language_summary: This would be the world's first binding international AI treaty covering human rights, but it's stuck in the starting gate: countries have to formally ratify it before it counts, and so far (as of late Sept 2026) only the EU itself has actually done so, even though 21 signatories including the UK, US, and Switzerland have signed on in principle. It has zero legal 'Parties' and creates no obligations yet.
verification_notes: Confirmed via an independent tracker (regulatorik.ai) and a law-focused blog (nicfab.eu), not just coe.int itself, both agreeing: only EU ratified, still zero Parties, not in force as of Sept 2026. Agent 1's ambiguous note about 'ratification math' is resolved: it's simply that a ratification alone doesn't make a Party until the treaty enters into force, and only 1 of the needed 5 ratifications (3 of which must be CoE member states — the EU is not a CoE member state) exists so far. Category 'Draft legislation pending' remains the best fit of the 5 labels; agree with Agent 1's judgment call. Confidence raised to high given clean independent corroboration.

key_instruments: UNGA Resolution on 'Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy AI' (March 2024); Global Digital Compact (Sept 2024); UNGA Resolution A/RES/79/325 (Aug 2025) creating the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and the Global Dialogue on AI Governance; separate Dec 2024 resolution on military AI
scope: global, all AI systems at a high level — mostly institution-building and shared principles rather than rules for specific systems
enforcement_mechanism: no — these are UN resolutions and compacts with no binding force and no penalties; the Scientific Panel produces research/assessments and the Global Dialogue is a negotiating forum, neither has enforcement power
effective_date_or_status: Resolutions adopted March 2024, Sept 2024, Dec 2024, and Aug 2025; the 40-member Scientific Panel (co-chaired by Yoshua Bengio and Maria Ressa) was appointed by the UNGA in Feb 2026, held its first virtual meeting in early March 2026 and its first in-person meeting in Madrid in April 2026, and released a Preliminary Report on 1 Jul 2026; the Global Dialogue on AI Governance held its first session in Geneva on 6-7 Jul 2026 — both bodies are now operating, not merely 'standing up'
plain_language_summary: The UN has gotten nearly every country in the world to agree, on paper, that AI should be safe and beneficial. Its new expert panel (co-led by AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio and journalist Maria Ressa) held its first meetings in early-to-mid 2026 and published a first report on AI risks in July 2026, and a new annual forum for governments to discuss AI governance held its first Geneva session in July 2026. None of this creates enforceable rules — it's diplomacy and shared research, not law.

enforcement_mechanism: no legal enforcement — voluntary code of conduct; companies self-report against it via an OECD-hosted monitoring framework

Over 50 companies including Google, OpenAI and Microsoft have signed on, and the OECD streamlined the reporting process again in May 2026 to make it easier for smaller companies to join too.

region_or_country: Global Partnership on AI (GPAI) / Bletchley Declaration & AI Safety Summit process
key_instruments: Bletchley Declaration (Nov 2023, signed by 28 countries + EU); follow-on Seoul (2024) and Paris (2025) AI Safety Summits; Global Partnership on AI, which merged into the OECD in 2024
scope: advanced/'frontier' AI systems and general international AI-safety cooperation; not a comprehensive rulebook for everyday AI use
enforcement_mechanism: no — declarations and summit commitments with no fines or licensing; produced some shared outputs (e.g. a network of national AI Safety Institutes) but no binding enforcement
